title: Leaf litter temperatures predict the green anole’s poleward range limit
text:
We hypothesize that the green anole’s poleward range edge is set not by the cold air temperatures in the canopy, but by the thermal conditions within the leaf litter where lizards overwinter. To test this, we combine biophysical models with mechanistic envelope models in four steps:

We define the green anole’s range using curated iNaturalist observations.
We obtain spatially explicit data on forest cover, elevation, and minimum and maximum temperatures across southeastern North America.
We use biophysical models to transform these macroclimatic data into the minimum annual body (i.e., operative) temperatures a green anole would experience in the canopy and at different depths in the leaf litter, and validate these estimates with data from our operative temperature models (OTMs).
We use mechanistic envelope models to evaluate which microclimate and forest cover threshold best predict the green anole’s range, both across its entire range and near its poleward range edge.

library(terra)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(TrenchR)

library(ggpubr)
library(geosphere)

text:
Defining the green anole’s range
We downloaded all research-quality iNaturalist observations of the green anole (Anolis carolinensis). Below we present the structure of the raw data, which is stored in the data folder:

# load occurrence data
caro_inat_data <- readRDS("data/caro_inat_data.rds")

We use the occurence data to define the green anole’s range. To do this, we first curate the original dataset by:

Rounding coordinates to one decimal place.
Removing observations with low positional accuracy (positional uncertainty > 1 km).
Filtering to the native range of the green anole defined by the following bounding box: longitude between -110 and -70 W, latitude between 22.5 and 37.5 N.
Adding up all observations within every 0.1 x 0.1 degree grid cell and keeping only cells with at least 3 observations. The goal of this step is to eliminate stand-alone observations caused by potential errors or rare occurrences.
Removing outliers based on distance to other observations. Any observation is considered an outlier if there are fewer than 3 observations within 50 km.

Lastly, we use the curated occurrence data to manually define the green anole’s range using the mapedit package.


Curate iNat data and define green anole range
## Note: This code chunk is not evaluated as it requires manual interaction
## to define the green anole's range using the `mapedit` package. The resulting
## range points are saved as an RDS file for later use.

# load packages
library(mapview)
library(mapedit)

# round coordinates and remove observations with low positional accuracy
caro_occ_data <- caro_inat_data |>
  mutate(
    lat = round(latitude, 1), lon = round(longitude, 1),
  ) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(positional_accuracy) & positional_accuracy <= 1000
  ) |>
  group_by(lon, lat) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n > 2) |>
  select(lon, lat)

# filter data to native range of green anole
caro_occ_data <- caro_occ_data |>
  filter(
    lon > -110 & lon < -70, lat > 22.5 & lat < 37.5
  )

# remove outliers based on distance to other observations
caro_occ_data$is_outlier <- apply(
  caro_occ_data[, c("lon", "lat")], 1, function(x) {
    distances <- geosphere::distm(
      x,
      caro_occ_data[, c("lon", "lat")],
      fun = geosphere::distHaversine
    )
    # if there are fewer than 3 observations within 50 km, mark as outlier
    if (length(distances) > 0 && sum(distances < 50000) < 3) {
      1
    } else {
      0
    }
  }
)

# save curated occurrence data
saveRDS(caro_occ_data, "data/caro_occ_data.rds")

# transform into a spatial object
caro_occ_sf <- st_as_sf(
  caro_occ_data[caro_occ_data$is_outlier == 0, ],
  coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  crs = 4326
)

# manually draw map around range
mapviewOptions(fgb = FALSE)
caro_range_sf <- editMap(mapview(caro_occ_sf))

# transform into a polygon object
caro_range_sf <- st_as_sf(caro_range_sf$finished)

# filter data to only include points within the continental US
caro_range_sf <- st_intersection(
  caro_range_sf,
  ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") |>
    filter(admin %in% c("United States of America", "Mexico")) |>
    st_crop(xmin = -125, xmax = -65, ymin = 20, ymax = 50)
)

# change the spatial resolution of the polygon to 0.04166667 degrees (~5 km)
caro_range_sf <- st_transform(caro_range_sf, crs = 4326)

# combine into a single (multi)polygon suitable for masking other layers
caro_range_poly <- st_as_sf(caro_range_sf) |>
  st_union() |>
  st_make_valid() |>
  st_as_sf()

# save caro range
saveRDS(caro_range_poly, "data/caro_range.rds")

Plot the native range and occurrence data of the green anole

caro_range <- readRDS("data/caro_range.rds")
caro_occ_data <- readRDS("data/caro_occ_data.rds")

# plot
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(
    data = map_data("world"),
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "lightgray", color = "darkgray"
  ) +

    data = map_data("state"),
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),

  ) +
  geom_sf(
    data = caro_range,
    fill = "forestgreen", color = NA, alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = caro_occ_data,
    aes(x = lon, y = lat, color = as.factor(is_outlier)),
    size = 1, alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("darkgreen", "darkred"),
    labels = c("In Range", "Outlier")
  ) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-101, -75), ylim = c(24, 37.5)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(-100, -75, by = 5),
    labels = function(x) paste0(abs(x), "°W"),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(25, 37.5, by = 2.5),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "°N"),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_blank(),

text:
Obtaining and processing ecological data
Next, we obtain the layers of ecological data we will need for the biophysical models. These include:

Forest cover: A raster layer representing the proportion of land covered by forests in each spatial cell. We obtained this data using the landcover function of the geodata package and combined the outputs of running this function setting var to "trees", "mangroves", and "wetlands". This data is, by default, offered at a 30 arc-second resolution. As part of our processing, we aggregated it to a 2.5 arc-minute resolution to match the resolution of the climate data.
Elevation: A raster layer representing the elevation of each spatial cell. We obtained this data from the WorldClim database at a 2.5 arc-minute resolution.
Minimum and maximum temperatures: Raster layers representing the minimum and maximum temperatures for each spatial cell. We obtained this data from the WorldClim database at a 2.5 arc-minute resolution.

We masked all ecological data to the spatial extent of the green anole’s range polygon + 2 degrees in all directions to have a representative sample of areas where the species does and does not occur. Further, we masked the rasters to only land areas within the continental United States and Mexico, the two countries were green anoles are considerd to be native.
Lastly, we add the species presence data to the ecological layers and save the resulting dataset (eco_df) as an RDS file for later use. The file is available in the data folder.


Obtaining and processing ecological data
## Note: This code chunk is not evaluated as it requires large raster files
## that are not included in the repository. The output of this code chunk is
## saved as an RDS file for later use.

# define land polygon
land_edge <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") |>
  filter(admin %in% c("United States of America", "Mexico")) |>
  st_transform(crs = 4326)

# crop the land polygon to the area surrounding the green anole range
range_extent <- terra::ext(
  st_bbox(caro_range_poly)["xmin"] - 2,
  st_bbox(caro_range_poly)["xmax"] + 2,
  st_bbox(caro_range_poly)["ymin"] - 2,
  st_bbox(caro_range_poly)["ymax"] + 2
)

# crop land edge
land_edge <- land_edge |>
  terra::vect() |>
  terra::crop(range_extent) |>
  st_as_sf()

# read and process vegetation rasters
trees <- terra::rast("raw_data/trees.tif")
mangroves <- terra::rast("raw_data/mangroves.tif")
wetlands <- terra::rast("raw_data/wetlands.tif")
veg <- trees + mangroves + wetlands
veg <- terra::mask(veg, land_edge)
veg <- terra::crop(veg, range_extent)
# 30'' to 2.5'
veg <- terra::aggregate(veg, fact = 5, fun = "mean", na.rm = TRUE)

# read and process elevation raster
elev <- terra::rast("raw_data/elev.tif")
elev <- terra::mask(elev, land_edge)
elev <- terra::crop(elev, range_extent)

# read and process tmin and tmax rasters
tmin <- terra::rast("raw_data/tmin.tif")
tmin <- terra::mask(tmin, land_edge)
tmin <- terra::crop(tmin, range_extent)
tmax <- terra::rast("raw_data/tmax.tif")
tmax <- terra::mask(tmax, land_edge)
tmax <- terra::crop(tmax, range_extent)

# match resultion of all raster
elev <- terra::resample(elev, veg, method = "bilinear")
tmin <- terra::resample(tmin, veg, method = "bilinear")
tmax <- terra::resample(tmax, veg, method = "bilinear")

# create a raster for green anole range
range_rast <- terra::rasterize(
  terra::vect(caro_range), veg, field = 1, background = 0
)
range_rast <- terra::mask(range_rast, land_edge)
range_rast <- terra::resample(range_rast, veg, method = "bilinear")

# combine all rasters into a single SpatRaster object
eco_rast <- c(veg, elev, tmin, tmax, range_rast)

# transform into data frame
eco_df <- as.data.frame(eco_rast, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
colnames(eco_df) <- c(
  "lon", "lat", "veg", "elev", "tmin", "tmax", "presence"
)
eco_df$presence <- ifelse(eco_df$presence > 0, 1, 0)

# save final ecological data
saveRDS(eco_df, "data/eco_df.rds")


Below we plot the ecological data for the green anole’s range, including forest cover, minimum and maximum temperatures, elevation, and species presence.


Plotting ecological data for the green anole’s range
eco_df <- readRDS("data/eco_df.rds")

# define common theme and axis labels for all plots
common_theme <- theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA),
    axis.ticks = element_line(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
x_axis_common <- scale_x_continuous(
  breaks = seq(-100, -75, by = 5),
  labels = function(x) paste0(abs(x), "°W"),
  expand = c(0, 0)
)
y_axis_common <- scale_y_continuous(
  breaks = seq(25, 37.5, by = 2.5),
  labels = function(x) paste0(x, "°N"),
  expand = c(0, 0)
)

# generate all plots
veg_plot <- ggplot(eco_df, aes(x = lon, y = lat, fill = veg)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "lightyellow", high = "darkgreen", na.value = NA
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-101, -75), ylim = c(24, 37.5)) +
  common_theme + x_axis_common + y_axis_common +
  labs(fill = "Forest\nCover")
tmin_plot <- ggplot(eco_df, aes(x = lon, y = lat, fill = tmin)) +
  geom_raster() +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-101, -75), ylim = c(24, 37.5)) +
  common_theme + x_axis_common + y_axis_common +
  labs(fill = "Minimum\nTemp. (°C)")
tmax_plot <- ggplot(eco_df, aes(x = lon, y = lat, fill = tmax)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis(
    option = "plasma", na.value = NA
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-101, -75), ylim = c(24, 37.5)) +
  common_theme + x_axis_common + y_axis_common +
  labs(fill = "Maximum\nTemp. (°C)")
elev_plot <- ggplot(eco_df, aes(x = lon, y = lat, fill = elev)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis() +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-101, -75), ylim = c(24, 37.5)) +
  common_theme + x_axis_common + y_axis_common +
  labs(fill = "Elevation\n(m)")

# combine all plots into a single figure
ggarrange(
  veg_plot, tmin_plot, tmax_plot, elev_plot,
  ncol = 2, nrow = 2,
  align = "hv"
)

title: Leaf litter temperatures predict the green anole’s poleward range limit
text:
Biophysical models

Functions & parameters

Solar radiation profile
We estimated direct hourly solar radiation (\(R_{solar}\)) as a function of geographic coordinates, seasonal timing and local topography. We first estimated the position of the sun throughout the year cycle (i.e., its ecliptic longitude \(\lambda\)) as a function of day of the year (\(DOY\)) and the Earth’s orbital eccentricity (\(e = 0.0167\)) as: \[
\lambda = \frac{2\pi}{365}\cdot(DOY - 80) + 2 \cdot e \cdot (\sin(\frac{2\pi}{365}\cdot DOY) - \sin(\frac{2\pi}{365}\cdot 80))
\]
Above, 80 is chosen to represent the day of the year when the vernal equinox occurs (typically March 21st). Using the ecliptic longitude, we then calculated the solar declination angle (\(\delta\)), which dictates day length and solar intensity as.
\[
\delta = \arcsin(0.3879672 \cdot \sin(\lambda))
\]
In the expression above, \(0.3879672\) is chosen to represent the Earth’s approximate average axial tilt throughout a year (arcsin(0.3879672) = 22.82\(^\circ\)). From this we calculate the sine of the solar altitude angle at a given hour of the day (\(a(h)\)) as a function of the latitude (\(lat\)) and the difference between the hour of the day (\(h\)) and the time of solar noon (\(S_n\)).
\[
a(h) = \sin(lat)\cdot \sin(\delta) + \cos(lat)\cdot\cos(\delta) \cdot \cos\left(0.2618 \cdot (h - S_n)\right)
\]
Where \(0.2618 \text{ rad h}^{-1}\) represents the Earth’s rotational speed (\(15^\circ h^{-1}\)). To obtain the time of solar noon at a given location in a given day of the year we used the solar_noon function from the R package TrenchR (Buckley et al. 2023). To account for the effects of elevation when computing the degree to which the atmosphere absorbs incoming solar radiation, we modeled barometric pressure (\(p_a\)) using an exponential attitudinal decay function.
\[
p_a = 101.3 \cdot e^{-Elev /8200}
\]
Combining \(\text{sin}(a)\) and \(p_a\) we then compute the path length of solar radiation through the atmosphere as:
\[
m_a(h) = \frac{p_a}{101.3 \cdot (\frac{1}{a_h})}
\]
Finally, hourly direct solar radiation (\(R_{solar}\), in \(\text{W m}^{-2}\)) is modeled by combining \(\text{sin}(\alpha)\), \(m_a\), the extraterrestrial solar constant (\(E_{sc} = 1.36 \text{kW m}^-2\)) with the atmospheric transmittance coefficient (\(\tau = 0.83\)).
\[
R_{solar}(h) = E_{sc} \cdot \tau^{m_a(h)} \cdot a(h) \cdot 1000
\]
We implement the function in R as follows:

# define constants
ecc <- 0.0167 # Earth's orbital eccentricity
spo <- 1.36 # extraterrestrial solar constant in kW m^-2
atc <- 0.83 # atmospheric transmittance coefficient

# define function
get_solar_rad_profile <- function(lat, elev, doy, solar_noon) {

  hours <- 0:23

  # calculate solar longitude and declination angle
  elon <- (2 * pi / 365) * (doy - 80) + 2 *
    ecc * (sin(2 * pi / 365 * doy) - sin(2 * pi / 365 * 80))
  dec_ang <- asin(0.3879672 * sin(elon))

  # calculate atmospheric pressure at the given elevation
  p_a <- 101.3 * exp(-elev / 8200)

  # calculate solar altitude angle
  geo_lat <- lat * (pi / 180)
  sin_alt_ang <- sin(geo_lat) * sin(dec_ang) +
    cos(geo_lat) * cos(dec_ang) *
      outer(solar_noon, hours, function(s, h) cos(0.2618 * (h - s)))

  # calculate air mass and solar radiation
  m_a <- p_a / (101.3 * (1 / sin_alt_ang))
  solar_rad <- spo * atc ^ m_a * sin_alt_ang
  solar_rad[solar_rad < 0] <- 0
  drop(solar_rad * 1000)

}



Air temperature profile
We estimated hourly air temperature (\(T_{air}\)) by interpolating between the daily maximum (\(T_{max}\)) and minimum (\(T_{min}\)) temperatures using a sinusoidal weighting function. We first defined the angular frequency of the diurnal temperature cycle (\(\omega\)) as:
\[
\omega = \frac{\pi}{12}
\]
reflecting a full cycle over the 24 hours of the day. From this we computed an hourly weighting coefficient (\(\gamma(h)\)), which determines the relative contribution of \(T_{max}\) and \(T_{min}\) to air temperature at a given hour of the day (\(h\)):
\[
\gamma(h) = 0.44 - 0.46\cdot\sin(0.9 + \omega \cdot h) + 0.11\cdot\sin(0.9 + 2 \cdot \omega \cdot h)
\]
Finally, hourly air temperature (\(T_{air}(h)\), in \(^\circ C\)) was calculated by weighting \(T_{max}\) and \(T_{min}\) by \(\gamma(h)\) and \(1 - \gamma(h)\), respectively:
\[
T_{air}(h) = T_{max} \cdot \gamma(h) + T_{min} \cdot (1 - \gamma(h))
\]
We implement the function in R as follows:

get_air_temp_profile <- function(tmax, tmin) {
  w <- pi / 12
  gamma <- 0.44 - 0.46 * sin(0.9 + w * (0:23)) + 0.11 * sin(0.9 + 2 * w * (0:23)) # nolint
  drop(outer(tmax, gamma) + outer(tmin, 1 - gamma))
}



Correct air temperature profile using vegetation cover
We corrected the hourly air temperature profile (\(T_{air}\)) to account for the buffering effect of vegetation cover on incoming solar radiation. We assumed that forest canopy intercepts a portion of direct solar radiation (\(R_{solar}\)) before it reaches the ground, cooling the air in proportion to both the amount of solar radiation available to be intercepted and the fraction of forest cover (\(C_{forest}\), ranging from 0 to 1) at a given location. We modeled this using a canopy cooling coefficient (\(\kappa = 0.007 \text{°C}\cdot(\text{W m}^{-2})^{-1}\)), such that the corrected hourly air temperature (\(T_{air}^{\prime}(h)\)) is:
\[
T_{air}^{\prime}(h) = T_{air}(h) - \kappa \cdot R_{solar}(h) \cdot C_{forest}
\]
Under peak solar radiation (800 - 1000 W m-2) and a fully closed canopy, this coefficient yields a peak daytime cooling buffer of 5.6 - 7 \(^\circ\)C. This range is consistent with empirical understory microclimate logger networks in temperate and subtropical forests (De Frenne et al., 2013, 2019; Zellweger et al., 2020) and standard surface-layer energy balance assumptions under suppressed convective mixing (Campbell & Norman, 1998).
We implement the function in R as follows:

# define parameters
cc <- 0.007 # canopy cooling coefficient (W m^-2)

# define function
correct_air_temp_profile <- function(
  air_temp_profile, solar_rad_profile, forest_cover
) {
  is_vec <- is.vector(air_temp_profile)
  if (is_vec) {
    air_temp_profile  <- matrix(air_temp_profile,  nrow = 1)
    solar_rad_profile <- matrix(solar_rad_profile, nrow = 1)
  }
  result <- air_temp_profile - 
    sweep(cc * solar_rad_profile, 1, forest_cover, "*")
  if (is_vec) drop(result) else result
}

air_temp_profile and solar_rad_profile may each represent either a single day (a vector of 24 hourly values) or multiple locations/days at once (a matrix with one row per location/day and one column per hour). The function first coerces vector inputs into single-row matrices so that the remainder of the computation can be written generically for both cases, then drop()s the result back to a vector at the end if needed. forest_cover varies by location (i.e., by row) but must be applied uniformly across all 24 hourly columns of solar_rad_profile. Because R recycles values column-by-column, multiplying the solar_rad_profile matrix directly by the forest_cover vector would misalign values whenever there is more than one row. sweep() avoids this by explicitly multiplying along MARGIN = 1 (rows), ensuring that each location’s forest cover value is applied only to its own row of hourly solar radiation values.


Surface temperature profile
We estimated the hourly surface temperature profile (\(T_{surf}\)) by adjusting hourly corrected air temperature (\(T_{air}^{\prime}\)) upward to reflect the additional heating that exposed ground surfaces experience from direct solar radiation (\(R_{solar}\)), relative to the surrounding air. We assumed that this surface heating effect is proportional to the fraction of ground not shaded by forest cover (\(C_{veg}\), ranging from 0 to 1), such that fully covered surfaces experience no additional heating while fully exposed surfaces experience the maximum effect. We modeled this using a surface radiative heat flux coefficient (\(\sigma = 0.02 \text{°C}\cdot(\text{W m}^{-2})^{-1}\)), such that hourly surface temperature (\(T_{surf}(h)\)) is:
\[
T_{surf}(h) = T_{air}^{\prime}(h) + \sigma \cdot R_{solar}(h) \cdot (1 - C_{veg})
\]
The surface radiative heat flux coefficient (\(\sigma = 0.02 \text{ °C}\cdot(\text{W m}^{-2})^{-1}\)) reflects the thermal response of dry organic leaf litter under low boundary-layer convective mixing. Under maximum unshaded solar radiation (800 - 1000 W m-2), this yields a daytime surface temperature excess of 16 - 20 \(^\circ\)C above ambient air, consistent with standard microclimate energy balance formulations (Campbell & Norman, 1998) and empirical forest floor microclimate measurements (De Frenne et al., 2019; Maclean et al., 2019).
We implement the function in R as follows:

# define parameters
srh <- 0.02 # surface radiative heat flux coefficient

# surface temperature profile
get_surf_temp_profile <- function(
  air_temp_profile, solar_rad_profile, veg_cover
) {
  is_vec <- is.vector(air_temp_profile)
  if (is_vec) {
    air_temp_profile  <- matrix(air_temp_profile,  nrow = 1)
    solar_rad_profile <- matrix(solar_rad_profile, nrow = 1)
  }
  result <- air_temp_profile + 
    sweep(srh * solar_rad_profile, 1, 1 - veg_cover, "*")
  if (is_vec) drop(result) else result
}



Above- and Below-ground (leaf-litter) temperature profile
To model the vertical temperature profile we defined separate functions for above and below the surface. Starting with above the surface, we assumed a smooth transition between the surface and the corrected air temperature measured at a reference height of 1.8 m (the reference height assumed by WorldClim). Following this assumption we first defined a dimensionless vertical profile function \(\phi(z)\) that would capture the relative influence of the surface temperature with height (\(z\)), as:
\[
\phi(z) = \frac{\ln\left(\frac{z + z_0}{z_0}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{z_{ref} + z_0}{z_0}\right)}
\]
Above we assume \(z_0 = 0.01\) m. This provides a small roughness-length offset added to avoid the singularity of the logarithm at the surface (\(z = 0\)). Then we, estimated the temperature at any height above the surface by applying this profile function as:
\[
T(z,h) = T_{surf}(h) - \left[T_{surf}(h) - T_{air}^{\prime}(h)\right] \cdot \phi(z)
\]
Below the surface, we modeled the propagation of temperature from the surface using the analytical solution to the one-dimensional heat conduction equation defined in Campbell and Norman 1998. To achieve this, we first calculated the thermal diffusivity of leaf litter (\(\kappa\)) from its thermal conductivity (\(k\)), bulk density (\(\rho\)), and specific heat capacity (\(c_p\)):
\[
\kappa = \frac{k}{\rho \cdot c_p}
\]
We parameterized \(k\), \(\rho\), and \(c_p\) using literature values representative of dry, loosely-packed organic leaf litter rather than mineral soil, since litter’s high porosity (\(\approx\) 80-90%) traps insulating pockets of still air that give it much lower thermal conductivity and bulk density than mineral soil. We set:

\(k = 0.05 \text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), within the \(0.04\text{-}0.06 \text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) range reported for dry organic litter layers (Campbell and Norman 1998; Oke 1987).
\(\rho = 150 \text{ kg m}^{-3}\), representing a slightly settled field-layer density within the \(60\text{--}180 \text{ kg m}^{-3}\) range measured for surficial \(O_i\) litter (Sato et al. 2004; Gaudinski et al. 2000).
\(c_p = 2500 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\), the standard value used for the dry solid organic fraction of soils (De Vries 1963; Bonan 2019).

Given the angular frequency of the diurnal temperature cycle (\(\omega = 2\pi/24 \text{ rad h}^{-1}\)), we then calculated the damping depth (\(D\)), i.e. the depth at which the amplitude of the surface temperature wave is reduced by a factor of \(e^{-1}\):
\[
D = \sqrt{\frac{2\kappa}{\omega}}
\]
At a given depth, temperature fluctuations are both damped in amplitude and delayed in phase relative to the surface. To account for this, we calculated the damping ratio (\(A(z)\)) and phase lag (\(\Delta t(z)\), in hours) as:
\[
A(z) = e^{-|z|/D}
\]
\[
\Delta t(z) = \frac{|z|}{D} \cdot \frac{24}{2\pi}
\]
Finally, temperature at depth \(z\) and hour \(h\) (\(T(z,h)\)) was calculated by damping the phase-shifted surface temperature (\(T_{surf}(h - \Delta t(z))\), obtained by linearly interpolating the surface temperature profile) around the mean daily surface temperature (\(\bar{T}_{surf}\)):
\[
T(z,h) = \bar{T}_{surf} + \left[T_{surf}(h - \Delta t(z)) - \bar{T}_{surf}\right] \cdot A(z)
\]
We implement the function in R as follows:

# heights and depths of interests
z_list <- zs <- c(seq(-0.2, -0.01, by = 0.01), 0, 1.8, 2)

# parameters
k <- 0.05 # thermal conductivity of leaf litter (W m^-1 K^-1)
rho <- 150 # bulk density of leaf litter (kg m^-3)
cp <- 2500 # specific heat capacity of leaf litter (J kg^-1 K^-1)
ref_height <- 1.8 # reference height (m)

# derived parameters
diff_sec <- k / (rho * cp) # thermal diffusivity of leaf litter (m^2 s^-1)
diff_hour <- diff_sec * 3600 # thermal diffusivity of leaf litter (m^2 h^-1)
omega <- 2 * pi / 24 # angular frequency of diurnal temperature cycle (rad h^-1)
damping_depth <- sqrt((2 * diff_hour) / omega) # damping depth (m)

# function to calculate temperature profile at different heights and depths
get_z_temp_profile <- function(z_list, surf_temp_profile, air_temp_profile) {

  # check if the input profiles are vectors or matrices
  is_vec <- is.vector(surf_temp_profile)
  if (is_vec) {
    surf_temp_profile <- matrix(surf_temp_profile, nrow = 1)
    air_temp_profile  <- matrix(air_temp_profile,  nrow = 1)
  }

  # define extended hours for interpolation
  hours <- 0:23
  surf_temp_mean <- rowMeans(surf_temp_profile)
  ext_hours <- c(hours - 24, hours, hours + 24)

  # calculate temperature profiles at different heights and depths
  z_temp_profiles <- lapply(z_list, function(z) {

    if (z == 0) {
      surf_temp_profile

    } else if (z == ref_height) {

      air_temp_profile

    } else if (z > 0) {

      a <- log((z + 0.01) / 0.01) / log((ref_height + 0.01) / 0.01)
      surf_temp_profile - (surf_temp_profile - air_temp_profile) * a

    } else {

      damp_ratio <- exp(-abs(z) / damping_depth)
      phase_lag <- (abs(z) / damping_depth) * (24 / (2 * pi))
      xout <- hours - phase_lag
      idx <- findInterval(xout, ext_hours)
      w <- (xout - ext_hours[idx]) / (ext_hours[idx + 1] - ext_hours[idx])
      ext_surf <- cbind(surf_temp_profile, surf_temp_profile, surf_temp_profile)
      shifted_temp <- sweep(ext_surf[, idx], 2, 1 - w, "*") +
        sweep(ext_surf[, idx + 1], 2, w, "*")
      surf_temp_mean + (shifted_temp - surf_temp_mean) * damp_ratio

    }
  })

  # combine the temperature profiles into a matrix
  names(z_temp_profiles) <- z_list
  if (is_vec) z_temp_profiles <- lapply(z_temp_profiles, drop)
  z_temp_profiles

}

The function above relies on several programming techniques to efficiently compute temperature at many heights/depths, locations and hours at once. lapply() iterates over z_list, evaluating a separate branch of the if/else if/else logic for each height/depth z, and returns the results as a list, avoiding an explicit for loop while keeping one profile (of potentially many rows/locations, by 24 columns/hours) per element. Because get_z_temp_profile() is a closure, the branches inside lapply() can freely access objects defined outside the function itself (e.g., damping_depth, ref_height) as well as arguments of the function itself (e.g., z_list) without having to pass them in explicitly. As with the earlier profile-correction functions, vector inputs are first coerced into single-row matrices so that the same matrix-based code handles both a single location/day and many at once, and drop() reverses this at the end when appropriate.
The belowground branch (z < 0) additionally needs to look up surface temperature at fractional, phase-shifted hours (e.g., hour - phase_lag) that can fall before hour 0 or after hour 23. To do this without treating the daily cycle as artificially bounded, hours is tiled into ext_hours, a length-72 sequence spanning the day before, the day itself, and the day after (hours - 24, hours, hours + 24), and surf_temp_profile is likewise tiled column-wise into ext_surf via cbind(). findInterval() then locates, for each shifted hour in xout, the index of the nearest surrounding pair of columns in ext_hours, and linear interpolation weights (w) are computed from the relative distance to each. sweep() is used again here, this time along MARGIN = 2 (columns), to apply a different interpolation weight to each of the 24 target hours while still allowing multiple rows (locations/days) to be processed simultaneously.


Operative temperature (body temperature) transformation
We estimated the minimum operative temperature (\(T_e\)) of a lizard (i.e., the steady-state body temperature reached at thermal equilibrium) across a range of above-ground and below-ground (leaf-litter) microhabitats. Because the coldest temperatures of a given day generally occur at night, this allowed us to assume that shortwave solar radiation was absent. Further, if the lizard is fully enclosed within the leaf litter, its view factor to the open sky drops to zero, all surrounding surfaces and boundary air are at ambient temperature, and radiative cooling to the sky is eliminated making \(T_e = T(z)\). Instead, if the lizard is aboveground, we assumed that \(T_e\) equilibrium, \(T_e\) is a conductance-weighted average of minimum ambient temperature in a given microclimate (\(T(z)\)), ground temperature (\(T_{ground}\)), and an equivalent radiant temperature (\(T_{rad}\)):
\[
T_e = \frac{h_c \cdot T(z) + h_k \cdot T_{ground} + h_r \cdot T_{rad}}{h_c + h_k + h_r}
\]
Where \(h_c\), \(h_k\), and \(h_r\) are, respectively, the convective, conductive, and radiative heat transfer coefficients. To solve for \(T_e\) when exposed, we first scaled body mass (\(m\), in kg) to a characteristic length (\(L\)) assuming standard reptile allometry:
\[
L = 0.02 \cdot m^{1/3}
\]
We then calculated the convective heat transfer coefficient (\(h_c\)) as the greater of forced convection (driven by wind speed, \(u\)) and free convection (driven by buoyancy):
\[
h_{c,forced} = \frac{10.3 \cdot u^{0.6}}{L^{0.4}} \qquad h_{c,free} = 3.5 \cdot L^{-0.25} \qquad h_c = \max(h_{c,forced},\ h_{c,free})
\]
We set wind speed to \(u = 0.1 \text{ m s}^{-1}\), representing the near-still boundary layer typical of sheltered forest understories at night, which minimizes forced convection and thereby amplifies the relative impact of radiative cooling. We treated conduction to the ground as a fixed empirical coefficient, \(h_k = 2.5 \text{ W m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-1}\), representing a small reptile resting against a solid substrate to maximize heat exchange.
Radiative heat transfer was linearized around the Stefan-Boltzmann constant (\(\sigma = 5.670374\times10^{-8} \text{ W m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-4}\)) and lizard skin emissivity (\(\epsilon_{lizard} = 0.95\), reflecting near-blackbody behavior of biological tissue in the thermal infrared):
\[
h_r = 4 \cdot \epsilon_{lizard} \cdot \sigma \cdot T_{air,K}^3
\]
The equivalent radiant temperature (\(T_{rad}\)) integrates thermal radiation from the night sky and the ground, weighted by their respective view factors (\(F_{sky}\) and \(F_{ground}\), each set to \(0.5\) assuming a flat, horizontal perching posture typical of a lizard when sleeping):
\[
T_{sky,K} = \epsilon_{sky}^{0.25} \cdot T_{air,K} \qquad T_{rad,K} = \left(F_{sky} \cdot T_{sky,K}^4 + F_{ground} \cdot T_{ground,K}^4\right)^{0.25}
\]
Where sky emissivity (\(\epsilon_{sky} = 0.75\)) represents a clear night sky, whose lack of cloud cover lets substantial longwave radiation escape to space, dropping the effective sky temperature well below ambient air temperature.
While it likely that some of the assumptions we take here are simplifications of real-world conditions, they provide a useful framework for estimating the operative temperature of a small reptile in a forest understory at night.
We implement the function in R as follows:

# parameters
sigma <- 5.670374e-8  # Stefan-Boltzmann constant (W m^-2 K^-4)
lizard_emissivity <- 0.95 # Longwave emissivity of reptile skin
sky_emissivity <- 0.75 # Longwave emissivity of the night sky
wind_speed <- 0.1 # Wind speed in m/s
f_sky <- 0.5 # Sky view factor above ground (50%)
f_ground <- 0.5 # Ground view factor above ground (50%)
convection_ground <- 2.5 # Conductive/convective transfer from ground

# define function to calculate operative (body) temperature
get_body_temp <- function(ambient_t, mass, in_litter) {

  # calculate derived values
  ambient_t_k <- ground_t_k <- ambient_t + 273.15 # C to K

  # characteristic length of lizard (m))
  l <- 0.02 * (mass / 1000)^(1 / 3)

  # forced convection (W m^-2 K^-1)
  forced_convection <- 10.3 * (wind_speed^0.6) / (l^0.4)

  # baseline free convection (W m^-2 K^-1)
  free_convection <- 3.5 * (1 / l)^0.25

  # total convection (W m^-2 K^-1)
  total_convection <- pmax(forced_convection, free_convection)

  # radiative transfer coefficient (W m^-2 K^-1)
  rad_heat_transfer <- 4 * lizard_emissivity * sigma * (ambient_t_k^3)

   # night sky radiative temperature
  sky_t_k <- (sky_emissivity)^0.25 * ambient_t_k

  # equivalent radiant temperature (°C)
  radiant_t <- (f_sky * (sky_t_k^4) + f_ground * (ground_t_k^4))^0.25 - 273.15

  # operative temperature above ground
  a <- (
    total_convection * ambient_t +
      convection_ground * ambient_t +
      rad_heat_transfer * radiant_t
  )
  b <- total_convection + convection_ground + rad_heat_transfer
  op_t <- a / b

  # return above or below ground based on `in_litter` parameter
  ifelse(in_litter, ambient_t, op_t)

}




Run biophysical models
Below we implement all the biophyscial modeling functions described above to estimate the minimum annual operative temperature of a green anole across 23 microclimates (20 leaf-litter depths from 1 to 20 cm, the surface, and heights of 1.8 and 2 m) in a typical year for every 2.5’ latitude and longitude spatial cell. Because minimum annual temperatures in the northern hemisphere typically occur in January, we use January 15 (doy = 15) as the representative day for our calculations.


Run biophysical models

  TrenchR::solar_noon,
  lon = eco_df$lon,
  doy = 15

  tmin = eco_df$tmin

  air_temp_profile = air_temp_prof,
  solar_rad_profile = solar_rad_prof,

)
surf_temp_prof <- get_surf_temp_profile(

zs_temp_profiles <- get_z_temp_profile(

# summarize zs temperature profiles into a data frame
micro_df <- Map(
  function(z_temp, z_val) {
    data.frame(
      lon = eco_df$lon,
      lat = eco_df$lat,
      elev = eco_df$elev,
      veg = eco_df$veg,
      presence = eco_df$presence,

    )
  },
  zs_temp_profiles, zs
) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  group_by(lon, lat, elev, veg, presence, z) |>
  summarise(
    min_annual_temp   = min(min_temp),

    .groups = "drop"
  )
micro_df$min_annual_body_temp <- get_body_temp(
  in_litter = ifelse(micro_df$z < 0, TRUE, FALSE),
  ambient_t = micro_df$min_annual_temp,
  mass = 3.1 # typical mass of a green anole (g)
)

# save the microclimate data frame
saveRDS(micro_df, "data/micro_df.rds")

title: Leaf litter temperatures predict the green anole’s poleward range limit
text:
Mechanistic envelope models
Envelope models compare the capacity of a set of threshold values across environmental variables to predict a species’ range. These models assign a binary suitability score to each spatial cell based on where the values of the environmental variables fall relative to the thresholds of interest. By comparing the inferred suitability map against the observed range cell-by-cell, we can obtain the True Skill Statistic (TSS), which evaluates model performance as a function of both sensitivity and specificity (i.e., its ability to simultaneously predict presence and absence):
\[
TSS = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} + \frac{TN}{TN + FP} - 1
\]
where \(TP\), \(FN\), \(TN\) and \(FP\) are the number of true positives, false negatives, true negatives and false positives, respectively. TSS ≤ 0 indicates a predictive ability no better than random, while a value of 1 indicates a perfect match. Thus, if a set of thresholds A yields a greater TSS than a set B, we can infer that the species’ range is more likely determined by A than by B.
Traditionally, envelope models rely on macroclimatic layers (e.g., air temperatures) and statistically identified thresholds. Instead, our mechanistic approach uses the minimum annual body temperatures estimated with our biophysical models for each microclimate and sets the threshold based on the green anole’s physiology. Specifically, we deem a cell unsuitable if the minimum annual body temperature in a given microclimate falls below 0 °C, which we assume is the lethal cold threshold for the green anole. Because the green anole is arboreal during its active season, we also include forest cover as a second variable, but we do not set its threshold a priori. Instead, we evaluate every forest cover threshold between 0 and 100% at 5% intervals. The combination of microclimate and forest cover threshold that yields the highest TSS is the most probable determinant of the green anole’s range.
What limits a species’ range at its poleward edge might differ from what limits it within its core. For this reason, we repeat the analysis across four spatial extents defined by the minimum annual temperatures in the canopy (1.8 m):

Entire range: all spatial cells for which we obtained estimates from our biophysical models.
Behavioral threshold: only cells where canopy temperatures fall below the retreating temperature we inferred from our surveys (Tret = 8.01 °C; see Green anoles retreat to the leaf litter to avoid extreme cold).
Soft physiological threshold: only cells where canopy temperatures fall below the lowest population-average CTmin of the species (6.8 °C).
Hard physiological threshold: only cells where canopy temperatures fall below 0 °C.

Below we classify every cell according to these thresholds and plot them.


Define thresholds for mechanistic envelope models
# estimate thresholds
thresh <- micro_df |>
  filter(z == 1.8) |>
  mutate(
    thresh = case_when(
      min_annual_temp < 0 ~ "below_zero",
      min_annual_temp < 6.8 ~ "below_ctmin",
      min_annual_temp < 8.01 ~ "below_tret", # Tret from leaf-litter-retreat.qmd
      TRUE ~ "rest_of_range"
    )
  ) |>
  select(lon, lat, elev, veg, presence, thresh)

# join micro_df with thresholds
micro_df <- micro_df |>
  left_join(thresh, by = c("lon", "lat", "elev", "veg", "presence"))

# plot thresholds
thresh_plot <- thresh |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lon, y = lat, fill = thresh)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_contour(aes(z = presence), color = "white", breaks = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(-100, -75, by = 5),
    labels = function(x) paste0(abs(x), "°W"),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(25, 37.5, by = 2.5),
    labels = function(x) paste0(x, "°N"),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "below_zero" = "darkblue",
      "below_ctmin" = "steelblue",
      "below_tret" = "lightblue",
      "rest_of_range" = "gray80"
    ),
    breaks = c("below_zero", "below_ctmin", "below_tret"),
    labels = c(
      "below_zero" = "< 0°C",
      "below_tret" = expression("< " * T[ret]),
      "below_ctmin" = expression("< " * CT[min])
    )
  ) +
  coord_quickmap(xlim = c(-101, -75), ylim = c(24, 37.5)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA),
    axis.ticks = element_line(),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.key.spacing.x = unit(0.5, "lines")
  )


Next, we run the mechanistic envelope models for every combination of spatial extent, microclimate and forest cover threshold, and store the resulting TSS values in a grid (tss_grid).

## Note: This code chunk is not evaluated as it takes a long time to run.
## The output is saved in the `data/tss_grid.rds` file.

# define TSS grid
thresh_names <- unique(micro_df$thresh)
veg <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.05)
zs <- unique(micro_df$z)
tss_grid <- expand.grid(
  thresh = thresh_names,
  veg = veg,
  z = zs
)
tss_grid$tss <- NA

# loop through
for (i in seq_len(nrow(tss_grid))) {

  # filter data of interest
  micro_df_sub <- micro_df |> filter(z == tss_grid$z[i])
  if (tss_grid$thresh[i] == "below_zero") {
    micro_df_sub <- micro_df_sub |> filter(thresh == "below_zero")
  } else if (tss_grid$thresh[i] == "below_ctmin") {
    micro_df_sub <- micro_df_sub |> 
      filter(thresh %in% c("below_zero", "below_ctmin"))
  } else if (tss_grid$thresh[i] == "below_tret") {
    micro_df_sub <- micro_df_sub |>
      filter(thresh %in% c("below_zero", "below_ctmin", "below_tret"))
  }

  tss_value <- micro_df_sub |>
    mutate(
      pred = min_annual_body_temp > 0 & veg > tss_grid$veg[i]
    ) |>
    summarise(
      tp = sum(pred & presence),
      fp = sum(pred & !presence),
      fn = sum(!pred & presence),
      tn = sum(!pred & !presence)
    ) |>
    mutate(tss = (tp / (tp + fn)) + (tn / (tn + fp)) - 1) |>
    pull(tss)
  tss_grid$tss[i] <- tss_value

  # track progress
  if (i %% 100 == 0) {
    message(paste("Processed", i, "of", nrow(tss_grid), "rows"))
  }

}

# save tss grid
saveRDS(tss_grid, "data/tss_grid.rds")

Lastly, we identify the combination of microclimate and forest cover threshold that maximizes TSS for each spatial extent (Table S8 in the manuscript) and plot the results (Fig. 4 in the manuscript). Panel A shows the areas below each threshold. Panel B shows the TSS values of every combination of microclimate (y-axis) and forest cover threshold (x-axis) for each spatial extent, with red circles marking the combination that maximizes TSS.
Across all spatial extents, leaf-litter microclimates predict the green anole’s range better than the canopy, with depths of 3-4 cm performing best. This effect is strongest in areas where canopy temperatures fall below 0 °C, where the poleward range edge is located: here, canopy microclimates have no predictive capacity (TSS = 0), whereas leaf-litter microclimates yield the highest predictive accuracy of all conditions tested.


Plot mechanistic envelope model results

title: Green anoles retreat to the leaf litter to avoid extreme cold
text:
Overview
Past studies, our own observations and many community-science reports on iNaturalist (Fig. S1 in the manuscript) suggest that green anoles retreat into the leaf litter during cold weather. Below we test whether cold temperatures trigger this behavioral shift and quantify how much the leaf litter buffers green anoles from cold. To do this, we combine standardized night surveys in Atlanta, GA, with temperatures recorded by operative temperature models (OTMs) deployed in the canopy and the leaf litter at five locations across the species’ range.
Each OTM consisted of an iButton suspended within a 2 x 7 cm painted copper pipe, secured with corks. OTMs with these characteristics match the thermal properties of similarly sized Anolis lizards and thus closely approximate the body temperatures lizards would experience in a given microhabitat. We affixed OTMs to branches at ~2 m height (i.e., “canopy”) or buried them 5-10 cm deep in the leaf litter, and programmed them to record temperature hourly between September 2025 and May 2026. The script used to process the raw iButton files (process-ibutton-data.R) is stored in the raw_data folder.

title: Green anoles retreat to the leaf litter to avoid extreme cold
section: Green anoles retreat to the leaf litter
text:
Green anoles retreat to the leaf litter
We conducted 27 standardized night surveys between September 2025 and January 2026 in a semi-natural area on the Georgia Institute of Technology campus in Atlanta, GA (33.75°N, -84.4°W), where green anoles are locally abundant. The site has small trees and bushes, interrupted by natural and artificial paths, and offers no other microhabitats for lizards to retreat to (i.e., no rock crevices or cavities in large trees) besides the leaf litter. In each survey, teams of 2-13 researchers walked a standardized 720 m transect for 1 hour, starting 1 hour after sunset, scanning vegetation for lizards and recording the time of each observation.
Below we summarise the survey data into the presence and number of green anoles observed per survey, and the operative temperatures recorded by the OTMs in the canopy and leaf litter during the survey period (i.e., between 1 and 2 hours after sunset, which we calculate with the suncalc package). We then plot how the probability of observing lizards (A) and the number of lizards observed (B) changed through time alongside canopy and leaf litter temperatures (Fig. S6 in the manuscript). Black lines represent the best-fit lines of Bernoulli (A) and Poisson (B) generalized linear models of observation probability and count, respectively, as a function of time.


Process survey and OTM data and plot them through time
otms_data <- readRDS("data/otms-data.rds")

# latitudes of locations
otms_data <- otms_data |>
  mutate(
    lat = case_when(
      location == "MIA" ~ 25.7617,
      location == "PSL" ~ 27.305,
      location == "ORL" ~ 28.5383,
      location == "GNV" ~ 29.6516,
      location == "ATL" ~ 33.7490
    )
  )

# predict CTmin by latitude
pred_ctmin <- tibble(
  lat = seq(25, 35, by = 0.1),
  ctmin = 57 - 1.68 * lat - 41.67 + 1.48 * lat
)

# read and summarize survey data
survey <- readRDS("data/sleepy-lizard-survey-data.rds")
survey_sum <- survey |>
  group_by(year, doy) |>
  summarise(
    count = n() - 1,
    presence = ifelse(count > 0, 1, 0)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    continuous_doy = ifelse(year == 2026, doy + 365, doy)
  ) |>
  filter(continuous_doy < (365 + 30)) |>
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(paste(year, doy), format = "%Y %j")
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# estimate sunset times for Atlanta, GA
my_year <- 2026
my_dates <- seq(
  as.Date(sprintf("%d-01-01", my_year)),
  as.Date(sprintf("%d-12-31", my_year)),
  by = "day"
)
my_lat <- 33.7490
my_lon <- -84.3880
sunset_times <- getSunlightTimes(
  date = my_dates,
  lat = my_lat,
  lon = my_lon,
  keep = "sunset",
  tz = "America/New_York"
)
sunset_times$doy <- yday(sunset_times$date)
sunset_times$mod_sunset <- hour(sunset_times$sunset) * 60 + minute(sunset_times$sunset) # nolint
sunset_times <- sunset_times |> select(doy, mod_sunset)

# filter otm data
otm_data_ATL <- otms_data |>
  filter(location == "ATL") |>
  arrange(id, year, doy, mod) |>
  filter(microhabitat %in% c("branch", "leaflitter")) |>
  left_join(sunset_times, by = "doy") |>
  # keep temperatures recorded during surveys (1 to 2 hours after sunset)
  filter(mod > mod_sunset + 60 & mod < mod_sunset + 120) |>
  mutate(
    year = year + 2000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    temp = ifelse(year == 2025 & doy < 200, NA, temp),
    temp = ifelse(year == 2026 & doy > 30, NA, temp),
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(temp)) |>
  group_by(year, doy, microhabitat) |>
  summarise(
    mean_temp = mean(temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_temp = max(temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_temp = min(temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(paste(year, doy), format = "%Y %j")
  )

# predict CTmin at ATL latitude
ctmin_atl <- 57 - 1.68 * my_lat - 41.67 + 1.48 * my_lat

# plot observation probability and OTM data
obs_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = c(1, 0, 6.8 / max(otm_data_ATL$mean_temp, na.rm = TRUE)),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = c("gray80", "darkblue", "steelblue"),
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = as.Date("2025-10-01"),
    y = ctmin_atl / max(otm_data_ATL$mean_temp, na.rm = TRUE) + 0.05,
    label = expression(CT[min]),
    color = "steelblue",
    size = 5,
    fill = "white",
    vjust = 1
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = filter(otm_data_ATL, microhabitat == "branch"),
    aes(x = date, y = mean_temp / max(otm_data_ATL$mean_temp, na.rm = TRUE)),
    color = "forestgreen", linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = filter(otm_data_ATL, microhabitat == "leaflitter"),
    aes(x = date, y = mean_temp / max(otm_data_ATL$mean_temp, na.rm = TRUE)),
    color = "darkorange", linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = survey_sum,
    aes(x = date, y = presence),
    color = "darkgray", size = 3, alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    data = survey_sum,
    aes(x = date, y = presence),
    method = "glm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    method.args = list(family = binomial(link = "logit")),
    color = "black", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.25
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Observation Probability",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(
      ~ . * max(otm_data_ATL$mean_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
      name = "Lizard Body Temperature (°C)"
    ),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2)
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "1 month",
    date_labels = "%b-%Y"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.border = element_rect(
      color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5
    ),
    axis.ticks = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.25),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 11)
  ) +
  labs(color = NULL)

# plot survey counts and OTM data
count_plot <- ggplot() +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = c(0, ctmin_atl),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = c("darkblue", "steelblue"),
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = as.Date("2025-10-01"),
    y = ctmin_atl  + 0.05,
    label = expression(CT[min]),
    color = "steelblue",
    size = 5,
    fill = "white",
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = filter(otm_data_ATL, microhabitat == "branch"),
    aes(x = date, y = mean_temp, color = "Canopy"),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = filter(otm_data_ATL, microhabitat == "leaflitter"),
    aes(x = date, y = mean_temp, color = "Leaf litter"),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = survey_sum,
    aes(x = date, y = count),
    color = "darkgray", size = 3, alpha = 0.75
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    data = survey_sum,
    aes(x = date, y = count),
    method = "glm",
    formula = y ~ x,
    method.args = list(family = poisson(link = "log")),
    color = "black", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.25
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name = "Green Anole Count",
    sec.axis = sec_axis(
      ~ .,
      name = "Lizard Body Temperature (°C)"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_date(
    date_breaks = "1 month",
    date_labels = "%b-%Y"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("Canopy" = "forestgreen", "Leaf litter" = "darkorange")
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.border = element_rect(
      color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5
    ),
    axis.ticks = element_line(color = "black", linewidth = 0.25),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 11),
    legend.position = c(0.98, 0.98),
    legend.justification = c(1, 1),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.key.spacing.y = unit(0.5, "lines")
  ) +
  labs(color = NULL)

ggarrange(
  obs_plot,
  count_plot,
  ncol = 1,
  nrow = 2,
  labels = c("A", "B"),
  align = "hv",
  # increase the size of the labels
  font.label = list(size = 16, face = "bold")
)









Next, we determine the temperature that triggers green anoles to retreat into the leaf litter. We focus on the presence of lizards rather than their abundance to account for the variation in the number of observers between surveys. We fit a generalized linear model with the formula:
\[
P \sim Bernoulli(p)
\]
\[
logit(p) = \alpha + \beta \cdot T
\]
where the observed presence of lizards (\(P\)) follows a Bernoulli distribution with an observation probability (\(p\)) that depends on the average operative temperature recorded across all canopy OTMs during each survey period, between 1 and 2 hours after sunset (\(T\)). The results of this model are presented in Table S5 of the manuscript.
From the fitted model, we then invert the logit function to obtain the temperature at which the observation probability equals a series of values of interest:
\[
T = \frac{logit(p) - \alpha}{\beta}
\]


Model observation probability as a function of canopy temperature
survey_sum_model <- survey_sum |>
  left_join(
    filter(otm_data_ATL, microhabitat == "branch"),
    by = c("year", "doy", "date")
  )

# model
mod <- glm(
  presence ~ mean_temp,
  data = survey_sum_model,
  family = binomial(link = "logit")
)
broom::tidy(mod)

Model observation probability as a function of canopy temperature
# get temperature thresholds for probabilities
probabilities <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.25, 0.5)
thresholds <- tibble(
  probability = probabilities,
  temperature = (log(probabilities / (1 - probabilities)) - coef(mod)[1]) / coef(mod)[2] # nolint
) |>
  mutate(
    temperature = round(temperature, 2)
  )

# define retreating temperature (Tret) as the temperature at which
# observation probability falls below 20%
tret_temp <- thresholds$temperature[thresholds$probability == 0.2]

thresholds |>
  kbl(

This value is just below the lowest canopy temperature at which we observed at least one lizard (8.89 °C). Below we plot the relationship between canopy temperature and observation probability, marking Tret, CTmin and 0 °C (Fig. 3A in the manuscript).

title: Green anoles retreat to the leaf litter to avoid extreme cold
section: The leaf litter buffers environmental temperatures
text:
The leaf litter buffers environmental temperatures
To quantify the thermal buffering green anoles experience in the leaf litter, we compare the minimum temperatures recorded by OTMs in the canopy and in the leaf litter across the five locations where we deployed them: Miami (MIA), Port Saint Lucie (PSL), Orlando (ORL), Gainesville (GNV) and Atlanta (ATL). We focus on January, the coldest month of the year, and obtain the minimum temperature recorded by each OTM on each day. Below we plot the average (± SD) of these daily minimum temperatures by location and microhabitat, with best-fit lines from a microhabitat-specific linear model (Fig. 3B in the manuscript).


Plot minimum temperatures in the canopy and leaf litter across latitudes
# summarise data
otms_data_sum <- otms_data |>
  mutate(
    year = year + 2000,
    date = as.Date(paste(year, doy), format = "%Y %j"),
    month = format(date, "%b")
  ) |>
  filter(month %in% c("Jan")) |>
  group_by(location, lat, id, year, microhabitat, doy) |>
  summarise(
    min_temp = min(temp, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# plot
buffering_plot <- otms_data_sum |>
  mutate(
    location = factor(location, levels = c("ATL", "GNV", "ORL", "PSL", "MIA"))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lat, y = min_temp)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = c(0),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "darkblue"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    linetype = "dashed",
    aes(yintercept = 6.8, color = "CTmin"),
    show.legend = TRUE
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    linetype = "dashed",
    aes(yintercept = tret_temp, color = "Tret"),
    show.legend = TRUE
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(color = microhabitat),
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    aes(color = microhabitat),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
    fun.data = mean_sdl,
    fun.args = list(mult = 1),
    size = 1
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = otms_data_sum |>
      group_by(location) |>
      summarise(
        lat = mean(lat),
        min_temp_mean = mean(min_temp[microhabitat == "leaflitter"]),
        min_temp_sd = sd(min_temp[microhabitat == "leaflitter"]),
        .groups = "drop"
      ),
    aes(x = lat, y = min_temp_mean + min_temp_sd + 0.5, label = location),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    vjust = -0.75,
    color = "darkgray",
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "branch" = "forestgreen",
      "leaflitter" = "darkorange",
      "CTmin" = "steelblue",
      "Tret" = "skyblue"
    ),
    name = "Microhabitat",
    breaks = c("branch", "leaflitter", "CTmin", "Tret"),
    labels = c(
      "Canopy", "Leaf litter", expression(CT[min]), expression(T[ret])
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(25, 35, by = 2.5),
    limits = c(25, 35),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.line = element_line(color = "black"),
    axis.ticks = element_line(color = "black"),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    legend.title = element_blank(),
    legend.position = c(0.98, 0.98),
    legend.justification = c("right", "top"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.key.spacing.y = unit(0.5, "lines")
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Latitude (°N)",
    y = "Minimum Lizard Body Temperature (°C)"
  )
buffering_plot









We then test whether minimum temperatures differ between microhabitats and across latitudes using a linear model with the formula:
\[
T \sim Normal(t_i, \sigma)
\]
\[

title: A major behavioral innovation enabled the poleward range expansion of a tropical ectotherm beyond its physiological limits
text:
Figure 1. Accounting for the American green anole’s (Anolis carolinensis) capacity to behaviorally exploit leaf-litter microclimates reconciles the apparent mismatch between its realized and fundamental cold-tolerance niche. (A) If we only consider estimates of lizard body temperatures (i.e., operative temperatures) in the above-ground canopy where anoles typically perch, the species’ range limit (solid green line) inexplicably extends into areas where minimum annual body temperatures would fall below its critical thermal minimum (CTmin; light blue) and even below freezing (dark blue). (B) However, accounting for behavioral thermoregulation resolves this paradox: mapping lizard body temperatures within the leaf litter shows that the species’ poleward range edge aligns cleanly with areas where subsurface temperatures fall below zero. (D) At lower latitudes within the green anole’s range (e.g., Miami), canopy temperatures rarely drop below CTmin, allowing lizards to retain their ancestral behavior of sleeping in branches (E) without physiological stress. In contrast, at higher latitudes (e.g., Atlanta), canopy temperatures regularly drop below zero during winter, forcing lizards to retreat into the thermally buffered leaf litter (F) to avoid lethal cold. Notably, tree cover (C) also acts as a crucial spatial determinant of this distribution, providing both active-season structural habitat and the leaf litter needed for thermal winter refuge. Credit to Jon Suh (E) and Flown Kimmerling (F). The code used to plot panels A-D is in raw_data/plot-figure-1.R.

This website contains the supplementary code and data for our manuscript on how the American green anole (Anolis carolinensis) managed to expand its range from the tropics into temperate North America.
The green anole descends from a tropical Cuban clade of arboreal lizards and is the only one of the >400 species in the Anolis genus to have colonized temperate environments. Yet, its physiological cold tolerance (i.e., its critical thermal minimum, CTmin) barely changes across its range, and most of its range regularly experiences temperatures below its CTmin, and even below freezing. Here, we show that the green anole resolves this paradox through behavior rather than physiology. In winter, northern populations abandon their arboreal niche and retreat into the leaf litter of the forest floor, which buffers them from lethal cold. Accounting for this behavior, rather than above-ground temperatures alone, predicts the green anole’s poleward range limit.
The analyses are organized into three vignettes that follow the structure of the results in the manuscript. In each vignette, code is folded by default (click on “Code” to expand a code chunk), and chunks that take a long time to run or require large raw files that are not included in this repository are not evaluated (eval = FALSE). For these, we save the output as an RDS file in the data folder, so every figure and table can be reproduced from the data included here.

title: A major behavioral innovation enabled the poleward range expansion of a tropical ectotherm beyond its physiological limits
text:
Vignettes and analysis

Green anoles live beyond their physiological cold tolerance: We compare the critical thermal minimum (CTmin) of green anoles across a latitudinal gradient with minimum annual temperatures and show that cold tolerance does not track climate. We then compare the green anole with 180 other lizard species and show that it is an exceptional case of a species living beyond its physiological cold tolerance limits (Fig. 2, S2, S3; Table S1-S4).
Green anoles retreat to the leaf litter to avoid extreme cold: We combine standardized night surveys with operative temperature models (OTMs) to identify the temperature at which green anoles retreat from the canopy into the leaf litter (Tret), and quantify how much the leaf litter buffers the minimum temperatures lizards experience across latitudes (Fig. 3, S6; Table S5-S7).
Leaf litter temperatures predict the green anole’s poleward range limit: We define the green anole’s range using iNaturalist observations, use biophysical models to estimate the minimum annual body temperatures a green anole would experience in the canopy and at different depths in the leaf litter, and use mechanistic envelope models to test which microclimate best predicts the species’ range (Fig. 4, S7, S8; Table S8).

title: A major behavioral innovation enabled the poleward range expansion of a tropical ectotherm beyond its physiological limits
text:
Datasets
The following datasets are used in this analysis and included in the data folder:

caro_inat_data.rds - Raw iNaturalist occurrence data for the green anole (Anolis carolinensis).
caro_occ_data.rds - Curated occurrence data for the green anole (Anolis carolinensis), with indicators for outlier locations.
caro_range.rds - Polygon defining the native range of the green anole (Anolis carolinensis).
ctmin_gradient.rds - Individual CTmin estimates (°C) and body mass of 95 green anoles from 7 locations across the species’ latitudinal range.
ctmin_lizards.rds - CTmin, elevational limits, substrate type (arboreal, semi-arboreal, other) and GARD range identifiers for 181 lizard species. Compiled from GlobTherm, SquamBase, Bodensteiner et al. (2024) and Salazar et al. (2025).
lizard_climatic_overfilling.rds - Latitudinal limits, total range area, and the area and proportion of the range below CTmin and below 0 °C for each of the 181 lizard species.
bio6_global.rds - Global mean (± SD) minimum temperature of the coldest month (BIO6) for every degree of absolute latitude.
sleepy-lizard-survey-data.rds - Night survey data from Atlanta, GA. Each row is either a lizard observation or, for surveys where no lizards were found, a placeholder row for the survey itself.
otms-data.rds - Operative temperatures (°C) recorded by operative temperature models (OTMs) deployed in the canopy (branch) and leaf litter (leaflitter) at five locations: Miami (MIA), Port Saint Lucie (PSL), Orlando (ORL), Gainesville (GNV) and Atlanta (ATL).
eco_df.rds - Forest cover, elevation, minimum and maximum temperature of the coldest month, and green anole presence for every 2.5’ cell across southeastern North America.
micro_df.rds - Output of the biophysical models: minimum annual ambient and operative (body) temperatures for every 2.5’ cell and microclimate (i.e., height above or depth below the leaf-litter surface).
tss_grid.rds - Output of the mechanistic envelope models: true skill statistic (TSS) for every combination of spatial extent, microclimate and forest cover threshold.

The raw data used to build these datasets (e.g., WorldClim and land cover rasters, GARD range maps, raw iButton files) are large and are not included in this repository. The scripts used to process them are stored in the raw_data folder alongside the raw files.

title: Green anoles live beyond their physiological cold tolerance
text:
Overview
Ectotherms are often assumed to need physiological adaptation to expand their ranges poleward. If that were the case for the green anole, its cold tolerance should track the colder climates it encounters at higher latitudes. Below we test this assumption in two steps. First, we compare how the critical thermal minimum (CTmin) of green anoles and minimum annual temperatures change across the species’ latitudinal range. Second, we combine CTmin data with the geographic ranges of 181 lizard species to quantify how much of each species’ range falls below its CTmin and below 0 °C, and assess whether the green anole is an exceptional case.

title: Green anoles live beyond their physiological cold tolerance
section: CTmin does not scale with climate
text:
CTmin does not scale with climate
Below we demonstrate how the critical thermal minimum (CTmin) of green anoles does not scale with climatic cooling. We do this by comparing empirical CTmin data with the minimum annual temperatures across a latitudinal gradient spanning the range of the green anole.
We collected the CTmin data from 7 locations across the range of A. carolinensis. To measure CTmin, we fitted lizards with a cloacal thermocouple probe, secured it to the base of the tail with surgical tape, and placed them in an experimental chamber submerged in an ice-water bath. Once internal body temperature stabilized after handling, we gradually cooled lizards and, starting at ~15 °C, evaluated the righting reflex at 0.2 °C intervals by placing the lizard on its dorsum and applying gentle pressure to the hind limbs. We recorded CTmin as the core body temperature at which an individual completely lost the capacity to right itself. We also extracted the minimum temperature of the coldest month (BIO6) from WorldClim and obtained the average, minimum and maximum BIO6 values for each 0.1° latitude band within a bounding box defined by the locations where we measured CTmin (+1° in each cardinal direction; +0.5° to the north).
The figure below (Fig. S2 in the manuscript) shows that while BIO6 decreases with latitude, CTmin does not follow this trend, indicating that green anoles are living in climates colder than their physiological cold tolerance.


Process BIO6 data and plot CTmin and BIO6 across latitudes
# read CTmin data
ctmin_gradient <- readRDS("data/ctmin_gradient.rds")

# read global min temperatures dataset
global_min_temp <- readRDS("data/global_min_temp.rds")

# define a search box for the bio6 dataset
search_box <- ext(
  min(ctmin_gradient$lon) - 1, max(ctmin_gradient$lon) + 1,
  min(ctmin_gradient$lat) - 1, max(ctmin_gradient$lat) + 0.5
)

# read in BIO6 data
bio6 <- terra::rast("raw_data/bio_6.tif")

# extract all BIO6 values and coordinates within the search box
bio6_data <- terra::crop(bio6, search_box)
bio6_df <- as.data.frame(bio6_data, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)
colnames(bio6_df) <- c("lon", "lat", "bio6")
bio6_df <- bio6_df |>
  mutate(lat = round(lat, 1)) |>
  group_by(lat) |>
  summarise(
    mean_bio6 = mean(bio6, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_bio6 = max(bio6, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_bio6 = min(bio6, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# plot CTmin and BIO6 data
ggplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "steelblue4", linetype = 2) +
  geom_jitter(
    data = ctmin_gradient,
    aes(x = lat, y = ctmin, color = "CTmin"),
    width = 0.1, height = 0,
    size = 3, alpha = 0.5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    data = ctmin_gradient,
    aes(x = lat, y = ctmin, color = "CTmin"),
    method = "lm", fill = "forestgreen", alpha = 0.2,
    show.legend = TRUE,
    fullrange = TRUE
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = bio6_df,
    aes(x = lat, y = mean_bio6, color = "BIO6"),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = bio6_df,
    aes(x = lat, ymin = min_bio6, ymax = max_bio6),
    fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.2, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    name = NULL,
    values = c("CTmin" = "forestgreen", "BIO6" = "steelblue"),
    labels = c(
      "CTmin" = expression(CT[min]),
      "BIO6" = "Min. Temp."
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = seq(-10, 20, 5),
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(1, 1),
    legend.justification = c(1, 1),
    legend.key.spacing.y = unit(0.5, "lines"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 15),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 14)
  ) +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(
      override.aes = list(
        linetype = c(1, 1),
        linewidth = c(2.5, 2.5),
        fill = c(NA, NA)
      )
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Latitude (°N)",
    y = "Temperature (°C)"
  )









Below, we perform a linear regression to test whether CTmin and BIO6 scale with latitude at the same rate. We combine both types of temperature values into a single dataset and fit the following model:
\[
T_i \sim Normal(t_i, \sigma)
\]
\[
t_i = \alpha + \beta_L \cdot L_i + \beta_C \cdot C_i + \beta_{L \cdot C} \cdot L_i \cdot C_i
\]
where temperature (\(T\)) depends on latitude (\(L\)), an indicator variable (\(C\)) identifying the nature of the temperature values (\(C = 0\) for BIO6 and \(C = 1\) for CTmin), and their interaction. If the interaction term (\(\beta_{L \cdot C}\)) is positive and significant, CTmin scales with latitude at a significantly shallower rate than BIO6. The results of this model are presented in Table S2 of the manuscript.


Linear model of CTmin and BIO6 across latitudes
# prepare data
bio6_df_model <- bio6_df |>
  select(lat, mean_bio6) |>
  rename(temp = mean_bio6) |>
  mutate(type = "bio6")
ctmin_model <- ctmin_gradient |>
  select(lat, ctmin) |>
  rename(temp = ctmin) |>
  mutate(type = "ctmin")
combined_df <- bind_rows(bio6_df_model, ctmin_model)

# fit linear model with interaction between latitude and type
lat_temp_model <- lm(temp ~ lat * type, data = combined_df)
lat_temp_fit <- broom::glance(lat_temp_model)

title: Green anoles live beyond their physiological cold tolerance
section: The green anole is an exceptional case of climatic overfilling
text:
The green anole is an exceptional case of climatic overfilling

Data processing
We compiled a dataset of CTmin and elevational limits for 181 lizard species, representing 17 families and 46 genera. We obtained CTmin estimates from the GlobTherm database and complemented them with two datasets focused specifically on Anolis lizards (Bodensteiner et al. 2024; Salazar et al. 2025). We then obtained elevational range limits, substrate use (arboreal, semi-arboreal or other) and the identifiers linking each species to its range map in the GARD database from SquamBase. The script used to compile this dataset (process-ctmin-lizards-data.R) is stored in the raw_data folder. For A. carolinensis, we set CTmin to 6.8 °C, the lowest population-average CTmin we measured (Knoxville, TN).
Below we present the structure of the resulting dataset, which is stored in the data folder:

glimpse(ctmin_lizards)

$ species        <chr> "Ameiva festiva", "Amphibolurus muricatus", "Anolis bar…

Below we combine data on the CTmin and elevational limits of globally distributed lizards to find the total area and proportion of each species’ range that is below their CTmin and below 0 °C. We also calculate the maximum latitude at which each species can occur above their CTmin and above 0 °C.
For each species, we:

Crop and mask global BIO6 and elevation rasters (2.5’ resolution, WorldClim) to the species’ range polygon from the GARD database.
Keep only cells whose elevation falls within the species’ elevational limits.
Convert each cell to its area in km2 (deg_to_area()), accounting for the fact that cells shrink with latitude because the Earth is an ellipsoid.
Sum the area of all cells, of cells where BIO6 < CTmin and of cells where BIO6 < 0 °C, and divide the latter two by the total area to obtain proportions.

Lastly, we calculate the global mean (± SD) BIO6 for every degree of absolute latitude, which we use as a reference in the plots below.


Calculate the area and proportion of each species’ range below CTmin and 0 °C
## Note: This code chunk is not evaluated as it takes a long time to run.
## The same code can be run locally to reproduce the results and the output
## is stored in the `data/lizard_climatic_overfilling.rds` file.

# read in global BIO6 tif
bio6 <- terra::rast("raw_data/bio_6.tif")
elev <- terra::rast("raw_data/elev.tif")
ranges <- readRDS("raw_data/ranges_vector.rds")

# filter ranges to only include lizard species with CTmin data
ctmin_lizards_ranges <- ranges[ranges$TaxonID %in% ctmin_lizards$gard_id, ]

# define function to convert lat-lon degree cell to km^2
deg_to_area <- function(lat, delta_lat = 2.5 / 60, delta_lon = 2.5 / 60) {
  
  # unit conversions
  lat_rad <- lat * pi / 180 # convert to radians

  # define constants
  equat_radius <- 6378.1370 # equatorial radius
  polar_radius <- 6356.7523142 # polar radius
  flat_factor <- 1 / 298.257223563 # flattening factor

  # radius curvature in the meridian
  e_sq <- (equat_radius^2 - polar_radius^2) / equat_radius^2
  denominator <- (1 - e_sq * sin(lat_rad)^2)^(1.5)
  m <- (equat_radius * (1 - e_sq)) / denominator

  # set length of 1 degree latitude in km
  km_per_degree_lat <- m * (pi / 180)
  lat_dist <- km_per_degree_lat * delta_lat

  # Calculate distance of 1 degree longitude along the parallel
  dist_km <- (pi / 180) * equat_radius * cos(lat_rad) / sqrt(1 - (2 * flat_factor - flat_factor^2) * sin(lat_rad)^2) # nolint
  lon_dist <- delta_lon * dist_km

  # Return cell area in km^2
  lat_dist * lon_dist
}

# define results list to extract data
results_list <- vector("list", nrow(ctmin_lizards))

for (i in seq_along(ctmin_lizards$gard_id)) {

  # get species range and ctmin
  range <- ctmin_lizards_ranges[ctmin_lizards_ranges$TaxonID == ctmin_lizards$gard_id[i], ] # nolint
  ctmin <- ctmin_lizards$ctmin[i]
  min_elev <- ctmin_lizards$min_elev[i]
  max_elev <- ctmin_lizards$max_elev[i]

  # crop BIO6 and elevation rasters to species range
  bio6_crop <- terra::crop(terra::mask(bio6, range), range)
  elev_crop <- terra::crop(terra::mask(elev, range), range)

  # filter all areas within range and within elevation limits
  valid_cells <- which(
    !is.na(bio6_crop[]) &
      !is.na(elev_crop[]) &
      elev_crop[] >= min_elev &
      elev_crop[] <= max_elev
  )

  # filter valid cells in BIO6 raster
  bio6_crop_filtered <- bio6_crop[valid_cells]
  bio6_crop_filtered <- bio6_crop_filtered$bio_6

  # extract coordinates of valid cells
  coords <- terra::xyFromCell(bio6_crop, valid_cells)[, "y"]
  dist <- deg_to_area(abs(coords))

  # get metrics
  total_area <- sum(dist)
  below_ctmin_area <- sum(dist[bio6_crop_filtered < ctmin])
  below_0_area <- sum(dist[bio6_crop_filtered < 0])
  below_ctmin_prop <- below_ctmin_area / total_area
  below_0_prop <- below_0_area / total_area
  max_lat_above_ctmin <- ifelse(
    below_ctmin_area %in% c(0, 1),
    NA,
    max(abs(coords[bio6_crop_filtered >= ctmin]), na.rm = TRUE)
  )
  max_lat_above_0 <- ifelse(
    below_0_area %in% c(0, 1),
    NA,
    max(abs(coords[bio6_crop_filtered >= 0]), na.rm = TRUE)
  )

  # store results in list
  results_list[[i]] <- data.frame(
    family = ctmin_lizards$family[i],
    genus = ctmin_lizards$genus[i],
    species = ctmin_lizards$species[i],
    ctmin = ctmin,
    substrate = ctmin_lizards$substrate_type[i],
    min_lat = min(abs(terra::ext(range)[3:4])),
    max_lat = max(abs(terra::ext(range)[3:4])),
    total_area = total_area,
    below_ctmin_area = below_ctmin_area,
    below_0_area = below_0_area,
    below_ctmin_prop = below_ctmin_prop,
    below_0_prop = below_0_prop,
    max_lat_above_ctmin = max_lat_above_ctmin,
    max_lat_above_0 = max_lat_above_0
  )

  # clear up memory
  rm(
    range, ctmin, min_elev, max_elev, bio6_crop, elev_crop,
    valid_cells, bio6_crop_filtered, coords, dist,
    total_area, below_ctmin_area, below_0_area, below_ctmin_prop,
    below_0_prop, max_lat_above_ctmin, max_lat_above_0
  )
  terra::tmpFiles(remove = TRUE)
  gc()

  # print progress
  cat("Processed species", i, "of", nrow(ctmin_lizards), "\n")

}

# bind rows for results and store data
lizard_climatic_overfilling <- bind_rows(results_list)

# change any NaN or -Inf values to NA across all columns
lizard_climatic_overfilling <- lizard_climatic_overfilling |>
  mutate(across(
    where(is.numeric),
    ~ ifelse(is.nan(.x) | is.infinite(.x), NA, .x)
  ))

# calculate global bio6 mean, min and max for every absolute lat degree
bio6_global <- as.data.frame(bio6, xy = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE) |>
  mutate(lat = round(abs(y), 0)) |>
  group_by(lat) |>
  summarise(
    mean_bio6 = mean(bio_6, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_bio6 = mean_bio6 - sd(bio_6, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_bio6 = mean_bio6 + sd(bio_6, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

saveRDS(lizard_climatic_overfilling, "data/lizard_climatic_overfilling.rds")
saveRDS(bio6_global, "data/bio6_global.rds")




Statistical analysis
To assess whether A. carolinensis is a unique case, we conducted an outlier analysis. Below we calculate Z-scores (i.e., the number of standard deviations above or below the mean of a group) for the area and proportion of the green anole’s range below CTmin and below 0 °C, relative to three groups: other Anolis, exclusively arboreal lizards, and all lizards in our dataset (Table S4 in the manuscript).


Z-scores of A. carolinensis relative to other lizards
# load datasets
lizard_climatic_overfilling <- readRDS("data/lizard_climatic_overfilling.rds")

# define function to get a Z-score for an observation relative to a group
get_z_score <- function(x, group) {
  (x - mean(group, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(group, na.rm = TRUE)
}

# get Z-scores of A. carolinensis with respect to other groups
caro_z_scores <- expand_grid(
  var = c(
    "below_ctmin_prop",
    "below_0_prop",
    "below_ctmin_area",
    "below_0_area"
  ),
  group = c("anolis", "arboreal", "all")
) |>
  mutate(
    z_score = map2_dbl(var, group, \(v, g) {
      dat <- lizard_climatic_overfilling[[v]]
      comp <- switch(
        g,
        anolis = dat[lizard_climatic_overfilling$genus == "Anolis"],
        arboreal = dat[lizard_climatic_overfilling$substrate == "arboreal"],
        all = dat
      )
      x <- dat[lizard_climatic_overfilling$species == "Anolis carolinensis"]
      get_z_score(x = x, group = comp)
    })
  )

# tidy up for display as a table
caro_z_scores |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = z_score) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(anolis, arboreal, all),
      ~ round(.x, 2)
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric = case_when(
      var == "below_ctmin_prop" ~ "Proportion of range below CT<sub>min</sub>",
      var == "below_0_prop" ~ "Proportion of range below 0 °C",
      var == "below_ctmin_area" ~ "Area of range below CT<sub>min</sub> (km<sup>2</sup>)",
      var == "below_0_area" ~ "Area of range below 0 °C (km<sup>2</sup>)"
    )
  ) |>
  select(metric, anolis, arboreal, all) |>
  kbl(
    col.names = c(
      "Metric", "Z-score (relative to <i>Anolis</i> genus)",
      "Z-score (relative to arboreal lizards)",
      "Z-score (relative to all lizards)"
    ),
    escape = FALSE,
    align = "lccc"
  ) |>
  kable_styling(
    full_width = FALSE,
    position = "center"
  )

We find that A. carolinensis has a much greater proportion and area of its range below CTmin and below 0 °C than other Anolis and other arboreal lizards, indicating that it is an exceptional case of climatic overfilling. Relative to all lizards, the green anole’s Z-scores are close to 0, as its overfilling resembles that of terrestrial, fossorial or saxicolous species living in colder climates, which can shelter from the cold in underground refuges.

  data |>
    filter(area_prop == metric_type) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = temp, y = value, color = substrate)) +
    geom_point(
      position = position_jitterdodge(
        dodge.width = 1,
        jitter.width = 0.2,
        jitter.height = 0
      ),
      show.legend = FALSE,
      alpha = 0.25
    ) +
    stat_summary(position = position_dodge(width = 1)) +
    geom_point(
      data = substrate_data |>
        filter(species == "Anolis carolinensis") |>
        mutate(
          below_ctmin_area = below_ctmin_area + 1,
          below_0_area = below_0_area + 1,

        pivot_longer(

            below_ctmin_area, below_0_area),

          values_to = "value"
        ) |>
        mutate(
          area_prop = case_when(
            metric %in% c("below_ctmin_prop", "below_0_prop") ~ "Proportion",
            metric %in% c("below_ctmin_area", "below_0_area") ~ "Area"
          ),
          temp = case_when(
            metric %in% c("below_ctmin_prop", "below_ctmin_area") ~ "CT[min]",
            metric %in% c("below_0_prop", "below_0_area") ~ "0°C"
          )
        ) |>
        filter(area_prop == metric_type),
      aes(x = temp, y = value, group = substrate),
      position = position_nudge(x = 1 / 3),
      color = "forestgreen",
      size = 4,
      show.legend = FALSE
    ) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 1.5, color = "gray70", linewidth = 0.2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = substrate_colors) +
    scale_x_discrete(
      labels = c(

    theme(

      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      strip.text = element_blank()
    ) +
    labs(
      y = y_label,
      subtitle = NULL
    )
}
